hints: Think about what the letters n.t.c. tell you - as temperature goes up, does resistance go up or down for this type of sensor?
Remember to put quantity and unit on each axis, and think about whether the fall in resistance is linear or gets less steep at high temperature.
walkthrough:
**Set Up The Axes Correctly**
You are plotting how resistance changes with temperature. So put resistance $R$ in $\Omega$ on the vertical axis and temperature in $^{\circ}\text{C}$ or $\text{K}$ on the horizontal axis. Both quantity and unit are needed for the sketch mark.

**Draw The NTC Shape**
For an n.t.c. thermistor, heating frees more charge carriers so resistance falls. Draw a curve that starts high at low temperature and falls with a negative gradient all the way. $$ R \text{ decreases as } T \text{ increases} $$ The fall is fastest at low temperature, so the curve is steep on the left and flattens on the right, staying above the temperature axis.

Final answer: Vertical axis: resistance $R$ in $\Omega$, horizontal axis: temperature $\theta$ in $^{\circ}\text{C}$ (or $T$ in $\text{K}$). Curve starts high on the left and falls steeply then more gradually to the right, with negative gradient throughout and not touching the temperature axis.

hints: Start with the sensor itself - what happens to the resistance of an n.t.c. thermistor when it gets hotter?
Look at where the voltmeter is connected - it is across the fixed resistor only, so think about how total current and sharing of the battery p.d. change.
walkthrough:
**What Happens To The Thermistor?**
Higher temperature means lower resistance for an n.t.c. thermistor. That is the key property you sketched in part (a).

**Follow Through The Potential Divider**
The thermistor and fixed resistor are in series across the battery. Total resistance falls, so total current rises: $$ I = \frac{V_{battery}}{R_{therm} + R_{fixed}} $$ The voltmeter reads the p.d. across the fixed resistor only: $$ V = I R_{fixed} $$ With $R_{fixed}$ constant and $I$ larger, $V$ increases. Equivalently, less p.d. is dropped across the thermistor, so more of the battery p.d. appears across the fixed resistor.

Final answer: Voltmeter reading increases. Resistance of n.t.c. thermistor decreases, so total circuit resistance decreases and circuit current increases. Hence p.d. $V = IR$ across the fixed resistor increases.

hints: Identify what strain of 0.020 means on the horizontal axis, remembering the axis is scaled by $10^{-2}$.
Read vertically up to the line and across to find the corresponding value of $\Delta R / R$ on the vertical axis, again noting the $10^{-2}$ scale.
Convert that fractional change into an actual change $\Delta R$ using the unstrained $120 \, \Omega$, then add it to find the new resistance.
walkthrough:
**Read The Graph For Strain 0.020**
Strain is $\Delta x / x = 0.020 = 2.0 \times 10^{-2}$. On Fig. 7.3 the horizontal axis is $\frac{\Delta x / x}{10^{-2}}$, so look at 2.0. Go up to the straight line and across. The vertical reading is: $$ \frac{\Delta R / R}{10^{-2}} \approx 9.0 $$ So: $$ \frac{\Delta R}{R} \approx 9.0 \times 10^{-2} = 0.090 $$

**Convert Fractional Change To Ohms**
Fractional change means change divided by the original $120 \, \Omega$ resistance: $$ \Delta R = 0.090 \times R = 0.090 \times 120 $$ $$ \Delta R = 10.8 \, \Omega $$ Stretching makes the wire longer and thinner, so resistance increases.

**Find The New Resistance**
Add the increase to the unstrained value: $$ R_{new} = R + \Delta R = 120 + 10.8 $$ $$ R_{new} \approx 131 \, \Omega $$ This is about a 9% increase, consistent with the graph.
Final answer: At strain $\Delta x/x = 0.020$, $\Delta R/R = 0.090$. $\Delta R = 0.090 \times 120 = 10.8 \, \Omega$. New resistance $= 120 + 10.8 \approx 131 \, \Omega$.
